summary:
When Earth is too far away to help, Moon-C is there.
On a mission to Mars, a reply from Earth can take up to 40 minutes to arrive, and in a medical emergency that can be far too long. Moon-C is an onboard health companion: a friendly, bilingual 3D character that listens, speaks and responds in the moment.
It monitors each crew member’s vital signs, from heart rate and oxygen to sleep, mood and radiation (simulated in this prototype), against ranges drawn from clinical guidelines and NASA health standards. When something is off, it alerts the crew and the medical officer. When a life is at stake, it guides anyone on board step by step through CPR, tourniquet application or choking response, with 3D demonstrations adapted to the ISS, the Moon, Mars or Earth. It also supports the mind, helping with stress, homesickness and low mood.
Its emergency decisions follow sourced rules, not generative AI, so it acts consistently even under stress. It runs offline on a single computer, keeps personal data private and queues reports for Earth. It never diagnoses, and its protocols await clinical validation: it exists so that no one on board faces an emergency alone.
details:
What does it do?
Moon-C is an onboard health assistant for space crews that works without internet. It helps every crew member monitor their health and act in time, without waiting for a reply from Earth. It shows each crew member’s vital signs live: heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure, respiratory rate, sleep hours, mood and radiation. When a value goes out of range, it alerts the crew and the Crew Medical Officer (CMO). It talks in English and Spanish, and an expressive 3D character guides anyone step by step through emergency maneuvers: CPR, tourniquet application and choking response. Each maneuver is adapted to the ISS, the Moon, Mars or Earth. Moon-C also offers emotional support for stress, homesickness or low mood. It queues data to send to Earth when a link is available. It never diagnoses: it compares values against a health manual and tells the crew member which steps to follow.

How does it work?
Wristbands, simulated for now, send vital signs every 2.5 seconds. Each value is classified as normal, attention or urgent, using ranges from published clinical guidelines (NEWS2, AHA/ACC, WHO, AASM/SRS) and NASA standards, adjusted for spaceflight. Every range cites its source.

In the chat, an intent classifier labels each message as emergency, health question, emotional support or casual talk. Health and emergency answers come only from the manual. A local AI model (Ollama, Qwen) handles casual conversation only, and a filter prevents it from naming diagnoses.

In an emergency, Moon-C opens the matching 3D guide and alerts the CMO. Each guide shows a proportional 3D mannequin, dedicated camera views, counts and a metronome. When the guide ends, a report with times, counts and a timeline is queued for Earth.

The character has rigged animations and facial expressions driven by a custom shader. Its states (calm, attentive, alert, listening, thinking, speaking, greeting) let the crew read at a glance what it is doing. Moon-C speaks with its own offline voice (Piper, with pitch and timbre tuned in Praat) and moves its mouth with the real audio volume.

Each function keeps working if another fails. If the server stops responding, the interface still detects emergencies with the same rules.

What benefits does it have?

  • Autonomy: a reply from Earth takes seconds from the Moon, but up to 40 minutes round trip from Mars. Moon-C gives immediate guidance.
  • Runs offline on a single modest computer.
  • Privacy: chat messages and audio are never stored, only measurements and safety logs. A crew member’s individual data is opened only during an alert, and every access is logged.
  • Bilingual: it answers in the language you write or speak in.
  • Mental health: it cares for the mind as well as the body, with a crisis protocol that alerts the CMO.
  • Safe by design: it never diagnoses, and every clinical answer and maneuver step is based on cited sources.

What is the intended impact?
To show that a crew can count on reliable, autonomous health support on long missions far from Earth. Next steps:

  • clinical validation of ranges and protocols by medical experts (maneuver steps are illustrative today);
  • connecting real wearables and dosimeters instead of the simulation;
  • adding local speech recognition so dictation also works offline.

What tools did you use?

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript (React) and JSON for the health manual and shared data.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic and httpx, with tests in pytest.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, Three.js and react-three-fiber, with tests in Vitest.
  • 3D: rigged GLB models with skeletal animation, facial expressions and a custom face shader, built with Blender and glTF-Transform. The character model was generated with Meshy AI, and the mannequins use the MakeHuman CC0 base mesh.
  • AI: Ollama with Qwen 3.5 (4B), run locally.
  • Voice: Piper (es_MX) and Praat (Parselmouth).
  • Other: Git and Git LFS.
  • Development assistance: Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic).

How is it creative?
Most health tools are dashboards. Moon-C is a companion: an expressive 3D character that turns data into calm, guided action. Its emergency guides change with gravity:

  • Microgravity: CPR starts with the Evetts-Russomano position and switches to the handstand method once the patient is strapped to the medical restraint system. Defibrillation is only advised with the patient secured, and rescuers rotate more often.
  • Moon and Mars: compression guidance adapts to partial gravity.
  • Sources: every guide cites its sources, including the AHA 2025 guidelines, the DGLRM/ESAM microgravity CPR guideline, Overbeek et al. 2022 and Thoolen & Kuypers 2023.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Alignment with NASA research: NASA’s Exploration Medical Capability defines the requirements for an onboard Clinical Decision Support System (HRP-48033) for Earth-independent missions. These include voice commands, an emergency interface mode, guidance for non-medical crew when the CMO is the patient, and reduced cognitive load. Moon-C is designed as the human interface layer of such a system.
  • Safety: no generative AI in medical decisions, no diagnoses, and cited sources for every range and maneuver step.
  • Reliability: offline-first, each function keeps working if another fails, and the same rules run in the interface if the server fails.
  • Privacy: minimal data retention and logged access.
  • Human factors: clear, short guidance under stress, a character the crew can read at a glance, and emotional support during isolation.
  • Transparency: all AI-generated content is labeled, and details are in AI_DISCLOSURE.md.
